location.value: Central and Eastern Europe: today’s Austria, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia, plus parts of Poland, Ukraine, Romania, Italy and Serbia. Ruled from Vienna and Budapest.

terrain.value: The Danube basin, the Alps, the Carpathians and the Hungarian plain, with a short Adriatic coast (Trieste, Fiume).
terrain.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

climate.value: Continental in the plains, Alpine in the mountains, Mediterranean on the Adriatic coast.

resources.value: Hungarian grain, Bohemian coal and industry, and timber.
resources.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

disasters.value: Food shortages and very high wartime inflation in the First World War (the price index rose from 129 in 1914 to 1,589 in 1918).

population.value: About 51.4 million (1910 estimate, summarised from Wikipedia).

urbanisation.value: Vienna (about 2 million) and Budapest were great cities. Prague and Trieste were also major cities.
urbanisation.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

disease.value: Not detailed in the sources checked.

migration.value: Large emigration to the Americas, especially from Galicia and Hungary, around 1880–1914.
migration.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

economicBase.value: Mostly agricultural, with industrial regions in Bohemia and Austria. It reportedly had the fourth-largest machine-building industry in the world.

tradeRoutes.value: A common customs union and rail network within the empire, the Danube, and the port of Trieste.

wealth.value: No GDP figure is given in the sources checked.

moneyAndTax.value: The gulden/florin (1867–1892), then the krone (1892–1918). Common costs were split between Austria (70%) and Hungary (30%), renegotiated every ten years.

inequality.value: Great noble landowners, especially in Hungary, and unequal political rights for different nationalities.
inequality.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

governmentType.value: A dual monarchy: two constitutional monarchies (Austria/Cisleithania and Hungary/Transleithania) in real union under one monarch, with shared foreign, military and finance ministries.

keyRulers.value: Franz Joseph I (1867–1916, Emperor of Austria from 1848). Charles I and IV (1916–1918, last). Foreign minister Gyula Andrássy.

succession.value: Hereditary in the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty. The heir Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in Sarajevo (1914).

institutions.value: The Compromise of 1867 (Ausgleich), the Imperial Council (Reichsrat) and the Diet of Hungary, each with its own parliament and government.

stability.value: Nationalist tensions between Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats, Serbs, Romanians and others, and constitutional crises in Hungary (1900s).

eliteConflict.value: Hungarian versus Austrian interests, renegotiated every ten years, and disputes over the army’s language of command.

armyAndTech.value: A multi-national common army and a small navy. Hungary supplied over 3.8 million soldiers in the First World War.

majorWars.value: Occupied Bosnia (1878) and annexed it (1908, the Bosnian Crisis). Declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914, starting the First World War. Defeated at Vittorio Veneto (1918).

territoryChange.value: About 621,538 km² (1905, summarised from Wikipedia). Gained Bosnia and Herzegovina. Broke apart in 1918.

alliancesRivals.value: The Dual Alliance with Germany (1879) and the Triple Alliance (with Italy, 1882). Rivals: Russia, Serbia and Italy (after 1915).

inventions.value: Vienna was a centre of medicine and science (Freud, Mendel’s genetics in Brno, Boltzmann).
inventions.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

scienceEducation.value: Strong universities (Vienna, Prague, Budapest, Kraków) and schooling in many languages.
scienceEducation.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

openness.value: Culturally rich and multi-national, but politically resistant to national self-government.
openness.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

religion.value: Catholic 76.6%, Protestant 8.9%, Eastern Orthodox 8.7%, Jewish 4.4% and Muslim 1.3% (1910).

languageWriting.value: German (at court) and Hungarian, plus Czech, Polish, Ruthenian, Romanian, Croatian, Serbian, Slovak, Slovene, Italian, Yiddish and others.

artsArchitecture.value: Fin-de-siècle Vienna: Klimt and the Secession, the music of Mahler and Johann Strauss, and Budapest’s grand architecture.
artsArchitecture.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

socialStructure.value: Aristocracy, a German- and Hungarian-dominated middle class, peasants, and many national minorities with unequal rights.
socialStructure.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the dynasty and Franz Joseph rather than to one nation. Motto: “Indivisibiliter ac inseparabiliter”.

neighbours.value: Germany, Russia, Italy, Serbia, Romania, Montenegro and the Ottoman Empire.

ideasReligions.value: A centre of modern art, psychoanalysis, music and economics (the Austrian School).
ideasReligions.source: Evans, The Pursuit of Power: Europe 1815–1914 (2016)

colonisation.value: No overseas colonies apart from a small concession in Tianjin (China). It annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina (1908).

riseSignals.value: Created by the 1867 Compromise after Austria’s defeat by Prussia (1866), to keep Hungary loyal.

peakPeriod.value: The stable decades around 1880–1908, with cultural flowering in Vienna and Budapest.

declineSignals.value: Unresolved nationalist demands, the Balkan crises, dependence on Germany, military defeats, and food shortages and low morale in the First World War.

outcome.value: Dissolution. In October–November 1918 it broke up into Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs (later Yugoslavia), with lands going to Poland, Romania and Italy.

sources.value: State statistics (1910 census), parliamentary records and diplomatic archives. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026 (the infobox was read word for word; the area and population figures come from a summary). See also Evans (2016).

overallCertainty.value: High for events and religion statistics. Some dates and names vary (e.g. the Compromise dated 30 March or 28 July 1867).
